title: The atomic bombs and the end of the war
log: 2026-11-04T09:36:52Z match: Claude Haiku 5.5 found no bank point the same, so it is written new

match.reason: The bank point covers the postwar world order and only mentions the bombs in passing, while the new point teaches the bombings and the historical debate over whether they were needed, so it is a different idea.

draft.title: The atomic bombs and the end of the war
card: In August 1945 the United States dropped an atomic bomb on Hiroshima, and then another on Nagasaki. Each bomb destroyed much of a city and killed very large numbers of people.
Japan surrendered a few days later, which ended the Second World War. Germany had already surrendered in Europe in May 1945.
Some historians argue the bombs ended the war quickly and saved lives that an invasion of Japan would have cost.
Others argue Japan might have surrendered without the bombs, or that the human cost was too great. Historians still debate whether the bombs were needed.
draft.remember: The bombs were followed by Japan's surrender, but historians still debate whether they were needed.

a.q: Which cities did the United States bomb with atomic weapons in August 1945?
opts: Hiroshima and Nagasaki
Tokyo and Osaka
Pearl Harbor and Manila
Hiroshima and Tokyo
a.why: The two atomic bombs fell on Hiroshima and then Nagasaki. Tokyo was damaged by other bombing but did not receive an atomic bomb.
a.clue: Two cities, one bomb each, in the same month.

b.q: Historian Ana says the bombs were needed to end the war quickly. Historian Ben disagrees. Which claim fits Ben's view?
opts: Japan might have surrendered without the bombs
Japan surrendered before the bombs were dropped
The bombs did not destroy any Japanese cities
Germany surrendered because of the bombs
b.why: Ben's view fits the argument that the bombs may not have been needed. The other options are false: Japan surrendered after the bombs, the bombs destroyed cities, and Germany had surrendered in May.
b.clue: Ben questions whether the bombs were needed.

b.best: Japan might have surrendered without the bombs

problems.detail: The right option is the only one with a qualifier ('might'). The three distractors are flat claims that are plainly false from the card, so a student could pick the hedged option without understanding the historians' debate.

check.summary: The facts check out and both intended answers are right. In question b, the right option stands out as the only hedged claim among obviously false ones, so the question is easy to guess.

b.q: Historian Ana says the bombs were needed to end the war. Historian Ben disagrees. Which argument supports Ben's view?
opts: Japan may have surrendered even without the bombs
An invasion of Japan may have cost far more lives
The bombs may have ended the war much more quickly
The bombs may have saved the lives of Allied soldiers
b.why: Ben doubts the bombs were needed, so he would argue Japan might have surrendered anyway. The claims about invasion deaths, a quicker end and saved soldiers all support Ana, because they argue the bombs did something no other path would have done.
b.clue: Which argument suggests the war could have ended another way?
